From the point of view of the employees however, the wage increase is good. The price of their basket barely rose with an increase in income (assuming that they have Chipotle in their basket).

Wouldn't the wage increase be essentially be negated because of the concurrent increase in the price of goods. I know that is assuming the worker only eats at Chipotle, but could arguably be extracted to all businesses that follow suit. Also it cost more for those not making 14% more. Right?

Correct on all accounts! However, this is assuming all price increases (in %) will be equal to wage increases (in %). I don't know the spreadsheet of Chipotle, but the 12% wage increase should not have been followed by a 14% wage increase, because their other fixed costs did not go up (unless they are making up for a backlog of cost increases).

By my logic (finished over half of an econ degree, so take it for what its worth), a wage increase should always be followed by a price increase, but the price increase should be less, in percent. This increases the buying power of those affected by the wage increase (lets assume only minimum wage employees wages go up, so we are assuming someone making $25/hr doesnt see an increase), but the buying power of the rich goes down. This causes them to go through more of their wealth, while the minimum wage employees go through all of their income. This causes money to circulate at a faster rate, helping the economy grow.

Wooh, lots of assumptions involved but this is the way that I see it. Not trying to instigate a fight.
I get it and I'm not taking this as a fight, just a gentlemanly discussion. This just seems like a cycle; one escalates and the other subsequently responds

Yeah! So, let's say MW (minimum wage) increases by 10%, so there is a P (price) increase across all goods by 8%. So, there is a MW increase by 8%, leading to a P increase of 6%. But then we neeed a MW increase by 6%, so there is a P increase of 4%. We can continue this ad nauseum, but this kind of looks like a convergent series, more specifically an infinite convergent series that can be expressed explicitly. This would result in a one time increase that reaches equilibrium.
